text: A skill added from a GitHub tree URL on a branch ref (`agntc add https://github.com/nuxt/ui/tree/v4/skills/nuxt-ui`, where `v4` is `refs/heads/v4` and the repo's tags are `v4.9.0`, `v4.8.2`, ..., none named `v4`) installs cleanly and records `ref: "v4"`, the branch-tip commit and no `constraint`; `update` and `list` then treat the stored ref as a semver tag, do a tag-existence lookup and report `Check failed — Tag 'v4' not found on remote`. It reproduces always, for any source pinned to a branch rather than a semver tag, leaving the entry permanently un-updatable.
how: Reported in the inbox bug and traced in discovery and the investigation's symptoms.

text: Severity differs by surface: `agntc update <key>` is a hard error that exits 1 (`update.ts:141`); `agntc update` (all) only warns loudly, since `check-failed` is excluded from `hasFailedOutcome`, and does not exit non-zero (`update.ts:597-603`, `623-631`); `agntc list` shows a permanent `✗ check failed` in its update-status column every run, with a degraded detail view and the "change version" action disabled (`list-detail.ts:133`). Synthesis validation corrected an earlier framing that `update`-all exits non-zero; the fix is unchanged by it.
how: Confirmed by synthesis validation against the code.

text: Impact is medium severity: no data loss, but the entry is permanently un-updatable with a loud recurring error; it affects any source distributed from a long-lived version branch, and breaks the invariant that anything installable is serviceable ("installed fine ⇒ should update/remove fine").
how: Assessed in the investigation's symptoms.

text: Is this a bug at all, or user error from feeding agntc the advertised GitHub tree URL instead of the `npx skills add nuxt/ui` shorthand?

It is a bug, whichever URL is better: agntc accepted the source, installed it and wrote a manifest it cannot then service, an internal-consistency defect where `add`'s ref resolution and `update`'s tag lookup disagree about what a ref is.
why: The invariant is "installed fine ⇒ should update/remove fine".

text: Did `add` record the ref wrongly, or is `update`/`list` mis-resolving a valid branch ref?

For the tree URL, `parseSource` sets `ref = "v4"`, `constraint = null`; `resolveTagConstraint` (`src/commands/add.ts:150`) fetches tags or derives a constraint only for a bare add or an explicit constraint, so with an explicit ref and no constraint neither runs, and `add` records `ref: "v4"`, the branch-tip commit and no constraint, as the version-constraints routing table prescribes for a branch ref without a constraint (track branch HEAD).
how: Code trace.

text: Install works because `cloneSource` (`src/git-clone.ts:34-38`) runs `git clone --depth 1 --branch <ref>`, which resolves either a branch or a tag; reinstall reuses it (`src/clone-reinstall.ts:327-340`), so a branch ref re-clones fine on update too.
how: Code trace.

text: `update` and `list` both go through `checkForUpdate` (`src/update-check.ts:57`; callers `update-check-all.ts:18`, `list.ts:123`, `update.ts:131/413`): with no constraint and a non-null ref, `isTagRef("v4")` is true, so it routes to `checkTag`, which lists remote tags and calls `findNewerTags(allTags, "v4")`; no tag is named `v4`, so it returns null and `checkTag` returns `check-failed` with `Tag 'v4' not found on remote`. Routed to `checkBranch`, the `ls-remote refs/heads/v4` lookup would have found the branch.
how: Code trace.

text: `add` records the ref correctly (`ref: "v4"` is the user's stated intent, to track the `v4` branch); the defect is entirely in how `update`/`list` classify the ref.
why: The code trace shows `add` doing what the routing table prescribes, and the update-check dispatch misrouting the branch to the tag lookup.

text: Two divergent ref-type classifiers exist: `isTagRef` (`/^v?\d/`, `update-check.ts`) and `isVersionTag` (`semver.clean(ref) !== null`, `version-resolve.ts:30`, used by `list-detail.ts:133`). They disagree on `v4`, `v4.0` and `4` (true for `isTagRef`, false for `isVersionTag`) and agree on `v4.9.0` (both true) and `main`/`dev` (both false); `checkForUpdate` uses the cruder `isTagRef`.
how: Code trace.

text: Root cause: `checkForUpdate` classifies a stored ref as tag or branch by the lexical heuristic `isTagRef` (`/^v?\d/`, `src/update-check.ts:39`); a branch named `v4` matches, is misrouted to `checkTag`'s exact tag-existence lookup, and fails permanently. The install path is ref-type-agnostic; update-check is the only path that pre-classifies the ref by string shape.
how: Code trace.

text: Ref type is inferred, never recorded: `ManifestEntry` stores `ref`, `commit` and an optional `constraint` but no `refType`, so `update` must guess whether `add` resolved a branch or a tag.
how: Code trace.

text: Install resolves refs by asking git (`git clone --branch`), while update-check pattern-matches the string and then does a type-specific `ls-remote`, so the two disagree whenever a name is ambiguous.
how: Code trace.

text: A branch name resembling a version tag is not exotic: distributing a skill from a long-lived major-version branch (`v4`, `v3`) is a common upstream pattern, and nuxt/ui ships its skill from `skills/nuxt-ui/` on its `v4` branch.
how: Observed on the nuxt/ui remote.

text: No test covers a branch ref whose name matches `/^v?\d/`; tests are believed (not checked) to exercise only real semver tags (`v1.2.3`) and clear branch names (`main`, `dev`).
how: Read from the code; the log says tests "likely" exercise only those cases.

text: The constraint-based routing added later by the version-constraints work was layered in front of the legacy tag/branch split without revisiting the `isTagRef` heuristic that governs unconstrained refs.
how: Code trace.

text: `isTagRef`'s own comment flags only the opposite failure (tags with a non-`v`, non-numeric prefix such as `release-1.0`), not a branch that looks like a tag.
how: Read from the code.

text: Every unconstrained branch ref that lexically parses as a leading-digit or partial version (`v4`, `v3`, `4`, `v4.0`, a date-branch `2024`) is misrouted to `checkTag`; `v4` is only the reported exemplar.
how: Read from the heuristic `/^v?\d/`.

text: A symmetric latent bug: a real tag whose name does not match `/^v?\d/` (`release-1.0`, `stable`) is misrouted to `checkBranch` and fails its `refs/heads/...` lookup.
how: Read from the heuristic and its comment.

text: `remove` is unaffected, as it does no ref resolution: the install and remove halves of the invariant hold, only update/check is broken.
how: Code trace.

text: How will update tell a tag from a branch when the branch is named `v4`?

Update-check determines a stored ref's type from remote truth, whether it exists on the remote as `refs/heads/{ref}` or `refs/tags/{ref}`, and dispatches to the branch or tag comparison by what exists, instead of guessing from the string.
why: From the string alone a ref's type cannot be known, and any lexical rule is a guess; the person twice made it the priority that update reliably tell a branch from a tag. Remote truth knows the type without a manifest migration, also fixes the symmetric `release-1.0` tag case, and costs little since update-check already contacts the remote via `ls-remote`.
rules_out: Swapping `isTagRef` for the stricter `isVersionTag` (still a lexical guess: a literal bare-major tag `v4` would be misread as a branch, and the `release-1.0` tag case stays misrouted)
Recording `refType` in the manifest at `add` time (new field plus a backfill for legacy entries, and it saves no network since update-check contacts the remote anyway)
alternatives: Option 1: swap `isTagRef` for `isVersionTag`
Option 3: record `refType` in the manifest at `add` time

text: What does the fix change, and what does it leave alone?
No manifest change: `ManifestEntry` gains no `refType` field, with no migration and no backfill; recording `refType` at `add` time is deferred as a possible future enhancement.
why: Not needed to fix the bug; update-check must contact the remote anyway.

text: No change to `add`, `remove`, or clone/reinstall: `add` already records the ref faithfully, and the install and remove halves of the invariant already hold.
why: The defect is entirely in update-check classification.

text: The `isTagRef` → `isVersionTag` swap is not implemented; it is retained only as a fallback one-line patch should a fix ever be wanted ahead of this work.
why: Still a lexical guess, and it does not clear the symmetric `release-1.0` case.

text: `checkConstrained` (entries with a constraint), `checkHead` (`ref === null`) and the `local` path are untouched, and the tag and branch comparison bodies keep their behaviour; only the routing decision between them changes. Constrained, HEAD-tracking and local entries must stay correct.
why: Those paths never went through `isTagRef`.

text: Vercel `skills` CLI shorthand compatibility (`npx skills add nuxt/ui` resolving to the right subpath) is out of scope, parked as the separate pre-existing inbox idea `vercel-skills-cli-compatibility`; bare `agntc add nuxt/ui` resolves at repo root and misses the `skills/nuxt-ui` subpath, a genuine but distinct gap.
why: A separate, pre-existing idea, not part of this fix.

text: In `checkForUpdate`, the first three dispatch steps (`local` when ref and commit are null, `checkConstrained` when a constraint is set, `checkHead` when ref is null) stay as they are; the lexical `isTagRef` split that follows is replaced by remote-truth classification, and `isTagRef` is removed, its comment not ported.
why: `isTagRef` has no other caller, and its comment documents only the opposite failure the fix clears anyway.

text: A non-null ref reaching the classifier is probed for both types in a single call, `git ls-remote <url> refs/heads/{ref} refs/tags/{ref}`, run via `execGit` with the module's standard `{ timeout: 15_000 }` like the sibling `ls-remote` calls, not `execGit`'s 30s default.
why: One call answers both types; the timeout matches `checkHead`, `checkBranch` and `fetchRemoteTagRefs`.

text: The probe output is classified by which of the two exact ref paths, `refs/heads/{ref}` and `refs/tags/{ref}`, appear: the full path is matched, never a prefix, so a ref with a slash cannot cross-match; the peeled `refs/tags/{ref}^{}` line and any other line are ignored; line order never matters.
why: An annotated tag adds a peeled line, and a loose match could cross-match slash-containing names.

text: A new small parser, returning the head sha and/or the tag sha keyed by exact ref path, reads the probe; it may live in `src/update-check.ts` or `src/git-utils.ts`, the implementation's call.
why: `parseLsRemoteSha` reads only the first line and `parseTagRefs` reads tags only, stripping `refs/tags/`; neither classifies a mixed heads-and-tags response.

text: Only `refs/heads/{ref}` present routes to the branch comparison; only `refs/tags/{ref}` present routes to the tag comparison. So a tag-looking branch (`v4`) and a plain branch (`main`, `dev`) check as branches, and a real semver tag (`v4.9.0`) and a tag not matching `/^v?\d/` (`release-1.0`) check as tags.
why: What exists on the remote decides the type, not the name.

text: Which type wins when the remote has both a branch and a tag with the stored ref's name?
When both `refs/heads/{ref}` and `refs/tags/{ref}` exist, the ref resolves deterministically to the tag and takes the tag comparison.
why: It mirrors git's own precedence (gitrevisions resolves a bare name in `refs/tags/` before `refs/heads/`); with no ref-type intent recorded, it is the principled default rather than a guess at what the installer meant.

text: Caret `^` and tilde `~` are the dominant operators across npm, Composer, Cargo and Bundler. text: How should a user express a version constraint at install time so it controls the scope (major, minor, patch) of automatic updates?

why: The user wants to control the scope of automatic updates; tag-pinned installs had no middle ground between pinned exactly and tracking HEAD.

text: Caret `^` pins the major and allows minor and patch updates: `^1.2.3` is >=1.2.3, <2.0.0.

text: Tilde `~` pins the minor and allows patch updates only: `~1.2.3` is >=1.2.3, <1.3.0. Composer's two-segment tilde wart (`~1.2` meaning <2.0.0) is not inherited.
why: Consistent across ecosystems with three segments; Composer's two-segment meaning is confusing.

why: Existing tag behaviour needs no change.

text: Partial versions fill zeros for both operators, following the `semver` npm package's conventions: `^1` = `^1.0.0`, `^1.2` = `^1.2.0`, `~1` = `~1.0.0`, `~1.2` = `~1.2.0`; caret and tilde semantics are stable regardless of segment count.

text: Resolution fetches all refs via `ls-remote`, keeps the semver-valid tags (non-semver tags excluded), and passes them with the constraint to `semver.maxSatisfying` to pick the best match; no custom pre-1.0 logic.

text: When several tags clean to the same version, the `v`-prefixed form is preferred (`v1.2.3` over `1.2.3`).
why: It matches the dominant tagging convention.

text: `semver.coerce()` is not used; `semver.clean()` plus `semver.valid()` is the pipeline.
why: `coerce()` is too aggressive and could match non-version tags.

why: Project-only detection fails on a brand-new project with no agent dirs yet, punishing a user who uses the agent extensively; the question is only whether the person uses the agent at all. Always asking with no detection is annoying for users of one agent.
rules_out: Project-level detection only
Always ask, no detection
alternatives: Option A: project-level detection only — fast, definitive, but fails on new projects
Option C: always ask, no detection — simple, but annoying for single-agent users

text: What's the right model for plugin ↔ agent compatibility: should the author declare which agents a plugin supports, or should the tool infer it from the plugin's asset types, and what happens when the user's agents don't match?

cites.section: What's the right model for plugin ↔ agent compatibility? > Context

text: Compatibility is declared by the plugin author through the `agents` field in `agntc.json`; the tool respects the declaration but never blocks the user. It is not inferred from asset types.
why: The author knows their plugin best — whether they tested it with Codex, whether it relies on Claude-specific features. Inference from structure is misleading: a skill tuned for Claude's sub-agents (as in technical-workflows) is format-compatible with Codex but won't work there.
rules_out: Asset-level compatibility inferred by the tool
alternatives: Option B: asset-level compatibility, the tool infers from asset types — zero config, but misleading

text: An agent is pre-selected in `add`'s agent multiselect only when both hold: the plugin declares it in `agents`, and it is detected on the user's system. E.g. `["claude", "codex"]` with only Claude detected pre-selects Claude, Codex available but not pre-selected; `["claude"]` with both detected pre-selects Claude only.
why: Pre-selection reflects both the author's declaration and what the user has.

text: Agents the plugin doesn't declare are still shown in the multiselect, with a warning that the plugin does not declare support for them — install at your own risk, it may not work — and the user can still select them. The user can always select any agent regardless of detection or compatibility: warn, never block.
why: "We're not the dad": the user might be about to install the agent, installing for a teammate, or inspecting the plugin. Always advise, never gate.

text: What does `agntc.json` look like for multi-agent?

cites.section: What does `agntc.json` look like for multi-agent? > Context

text: `agntc.json` holds a single required field, `agents` (`string[]`): the agent identifiers the plugin was built and tested for. Valid values are `"claude"` and `"codex"`.
why: The spec's schema, approved after the discussion, replaces the discussion's optional `type` + `agents` schema.

text: There is no default-to-all: the author explicitly declares which agents they support, and every installable unit declares its own `agents`, even within a collection — no inheritance.
why: The spec, approved after the discussion, replaces the discussion's default of compatible with all agents when `agents` is omitted.
rules_out: Omitting `agents` to mean compatible with all agents
Inheriting `agents` within a collection

text: `agntc.json` has no `type` field: skill vs plugin vs collection is inferred from directory structure.
why: The spec, approved after the discussion, replaces the discussion's `type` field.
rules_out: A `type` field in `agntc.json`

text: A missing `agents` field aborts with "Invalid agntc.json: agents field is required"; an empty `agents` array aborts with "Invalid agntc.json: agents must not be empty"; an unknown agent identifier warns and continues, the unknown value ignored during routing.
why: Ignoring unknown identifiers future-proofs against plugins declaring agents the tool doesn't support yet.

text: What happens on update when the new version's `agntc.json` declares different agents from those the plugin is installed for?

Update re-reads the new version's `agntc.json` and compares its `agents` with the manifest entry's. If the author dropped an agent: warn ("Plugin `{key}` no longer declares support for `{dropped_agent}`. Currently installed for: `{manifest agents}`. New version supports: `{new agents}`."), update only for agents still declared, remove the dropped agent's files with the nuke and not re-create them, update the entry's `agents` to what was installed, and say so in the summary ("Updated for Claude. Codex support removed by plugin author — Codex files removed.").
why: The author's declaration governs what an update reinstalls.

text: If all installed agents were dropped, the update is skipped with a warning: "Plugin `{key}` no longer supports any of your installed agents. No update performed. Run `npx agntc remove {key}` to clean up." Existing files are left in place; the user decides when to remove.
why: The update would effectively become a removal, which is the user's call.

text: What is the full `add` flow, from argument parsing through to the manifest write?

cites.section: What's the full `add` flow — from argument parsing through to manifest write? > Context

text: `add` takes exactly one source per invocation and the source is always required: there is no no-arg mode. Several plugins of a collection are chosen interactively within the flow, not passed as several arguments.
why: A source is copy-pasted from a README anyway, so an interactive "what do you want to install?" prompt adds nothing.
rules_out: A no-arg interactive `add`
Several sources as several arguments

text: GitHub shorthand is the primary source format: `owner/repo`, with an `@ref` suffix naming a tag or a branch (`owner/repo@v2.0`, `owner/repo@branch-name`).
why: The spec's own text and the log agree on `@ref`; the `#ref` fragment, `@skill` selection, subpaths and `github:`/`gitlab:` prefixes the spec now shows came from a corrigendum of the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit, which governs nothing.

text: Full git URLs are accepted: HTTPS (`https://github.com/owner/repo.git`, any git host) and SSH (`git@github.com:owner/repo.git`, for SSH auth setups).
why: The host restrictions and refused URL kinds the spec now shows came from a corrigendum of the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit; the spec's text before it read any git host.

text: A local path is a source: absolute, relative (`./my-plugin`) or `~/my-plugin`. There is no git clone; files are copied directly. Local paths have no ref.
why: For plugin development and testing without pushing to git first.

text: A tree URL pointing at one plugin within a collection (`https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/main/plugin-name`) is a source: the collection multiselect is skipped and that plugin installs directly, the rest of the flow (agent selection, collision check, copy) proceeding as normal. Its ref is carried in the URL path (`/tree/{ref}/...`).
why: A collection shortcut.

text: Every source format but a direct path and a local path can carry a ref. With no ref given, the newest semver tag is installed with a caret constraint, falling back to the default branch.
why: The spec's corrigendum records this as the version-constraints change, superseding the earlier rule that no ref meant default HEAD.
rules_out: Installing default HEAD when no ref is given

text: The manifest key is derived from the source whatever its format: `owner/repo` for a standalone plugin, `owner/repo/plugin-name` for a collection plugin; for a local path the resolved absolute path, and `{absolute-path}/{plugin-name}` for a local collection's plugin, with `~` expanded before storing.
why: The per-skill `owner/repo/<declared-name>` key the spec now shows came from a corrigendum of the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit, which governs nothing.

text: A corrigendum from the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit (2026-10-07) rewrote the spec's shorthand: refs and constraints in a `#` fragment, `@` selecting a skill by declared name, subpath shorthand and `github:`/`gitlab:` prefixes accepted. That unit is cancelled, so this is not current.
how: Read in the spec's Corrigenda and the Source Argument table it edited.

text: A corrigendum from the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit (2026-10-07) narrowed HTTPS sources from any git host to GitHub (incl. a `GH_HOST` host), gitlab.com and `/-/tree/` URLs, Azure Repos `_git` URLs and `.git`-suffixed URLs, refusing GitHub download links and other http(s) URLs. That unit is cancelled, so this is not current.
how: Read in the spec's Corrigenda and the Source Argument table it edited.

text: A corrigendum from the cancelled vercel-skills-compatibility unit (2026-10-07) changed the collection key to `owner/repo/<declared-name>`, one key per skill however it was selected. That unit is cancelled, so this is not current.
how: Read in the spec's Corrigenda and the Source Argument section it edited.

text: After parsing the source, `add` shallow-clones the repo into a temp directory, or copies from the local path, and cleans up the temp clone directory at the end (git sources only).
why: No history is needed: clone, copy, discard.

text: `add` then reads `agntc.json` and decides skill, plugin or collection by the structural type detection rules, not by a declared type field.
why: The spec replaced the log's `"type"` field and convention fallback with detection from structure.
rules_out: A `"type": "collection"` / `"plugin"` field in `agntc.json`
A convention fallback for repos without `agntc.json`

text: For a collection, `add` shows a multiselect of all its plugins. Already-installed plugins are marked but still selectable; selecting one triggers a reinstall. There is no separate `--force` flag.
why: Reinstall is nuke-and-reinstall, consistent with the update strategy.
rules_out: A `--force` flag
Greying out installed plugins so they can't be picked

text: `add` always shows the agent multiselect listing every supported agent (currently Claude, Codex), never skipped, even when only one agent would be pre-selected.
why: Auto-selecting hides the option to install for other agents; always showing it is one code path.
rules_out: Auto-selecting when exactly one agent is detected and compatible

text: In the agent multiselect, agents both detected and declared compatible are pre-selected; the others are listed unselected, those the plugin doesn't declare shown with a warning. The user can select any agent regardless: warn, never block.
why: Detection and compatibility guide the choice without gating it.

text: Selecting zero plugins in the collection multiselect, or zero agents, is a cancel: a brief message and a clean exit, not an error.
why: Nothing chosen means nothing to do.

text: For a selected plugin already installed, `add` deletes every file in its manifest `files` before proceeding, as update's nuke step does.
why: A clean slate: no orphaned files from the previous version and no conflict prompts against the plugin's own assets.

text: How should conflicts be handled across commands?
Conflicts are handled in `add` alone, the only command where they arise.
why: Remove and update work only on files the manifest already gives the plugin.

text: Before any copying, `add` diffs the incoming file list against every manifest entry. A path another plugin owns is a hard block: it shows which files conflict and which plugin owns them, and offers exactly two options, remove the conflicting plugin first then continue (both in one flow), or cancel.
why: Plugins are atomic with interdependent assets; overwriting one asset of a plugin breaks its internal wiring.
rules_out: An "install anyway" option
Overwriting another plugin's asset and transferring its ownership in the manifest

text: After the collision check and before any copying, `add` scans each plugin's destination paths on disk for unmanaged files (present but tracked by no manifest entry), detected at the asset level: an existing skill directory, agent file or hook file is one conflict each.
why: Asset-level granularity keeps the prompts manageable: one prompt per skill, not one per reference file.
rules_out: File-level conflict detection
Prompting as conflicts are met during the copy

text: Where a plugin has unmanaged conflicts, `add` shows all its conflicting assets and offers two options: overwrite all, after a second confirmation ("Are you sure? These files will be permanently replaced."), or cancel this plugin's install. Overwriting nukes each conflicting asset whole and replaces it, with no merging or diffing.
why: Plugins are atomic: overwrite everything or install nothing, no partial installs.
rules_out: Per-asset overwrite or skip

text: With several collection plugins selected, each is checked for conflicts independently: those without conflicts proceed, those the user cancels are excluded, and the summary notes which were skipped.
why: Each plugin is atomic and independent of the others.

text: All conflict resolution happens before copying begins, so no rollback is needed for it.
why: Resolving up front leaves nothing half-copied to undo.

text: For each plugin and each selected agent, `add` routes assets through the driver config and copies them to the target directories.
why: Routing is per agent driver.

text: `add` writes `.agntc/manifest.json` once, atomically, at the end: the new entries, replacing any reinstalled entries.
why: State changes are held in memory during the operation and written in one go.

text: `add` ends with a summary of what was installed, broken down per agent with asset counts (e.g. "Installed leeovery/claude-technical-workflows@v2.1.6", then "Claude: 12 skills, 3 agents, 2 hooks", "Codex: 12 skills"), repeated per plugin for collections, showing only the asset types actually installed (no "0 hooks" lines), and noting plugins skipped for conflicts.
why: Shows what landed where without noise.
rules_out: Per-plugin paths in a collection's summary

cites.section: How should `remove` work — interactive, parameterized, or both? > Context

text: `remove` is both interactive and parameterized: `npx agntc remove` reads the manifest and lets the user pick from all installed plugins; `npx agntc remove owner/repo` removes a standalone plugin, or every installed plugin of that collection; `npx agntc remove owner/repo/plugin-name` removes one collection plugin.
why: Parameters for power users and scripts, the picker as the friendly path; `owner/repo` on a collection is the "nuke the whole collection" path.

cites.section: How should `remove` work — interactive, parameterized, or both? > Decision

text: With no plugins installed, `remove` displays "No plugins installed." and exits.
why: Nothing to pick from.

text: `remove` always confirms before deleting: it shows the file paths to be removed and requires an explicit yes.
why: Deletion is destructive; the confirmation is the safety gate.

cites.section: How should `remove` work — interactive, parameterized, or both? > Decision

text: `remove` does no modification detection: no checksums are kept, and edits the user made to installed files are lost on removal.
why: Git is the safety net; storing checksums at install and comparing on remove adds complexity for a case git already handles, and the confirmation is enough.
rules_out: Storing file checksums at install time to detect modifications on remove

cites.section: How should `remove` work — interactive, parameterized, or both? > Decision

text: `remove` reads the manifest and identifies the target plugins from the argument or selection, confirms, deletes every file in each plugin's manifest `files`, removes the entry, writes the manifest, and shows a summary of what was removed.
why: Removal is manifest-driven.

cites.section: How should `remove` work — interactive, parameterized, or both? > Decision

text: `remove` leaves empty directories in place; agent config dirs (`.claude/`, `.agents/`) persist regardless.
why: Cleaning up empty dirs adds logic for marginal benefit.

text: What are the `update` semantics: per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once?

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Context

text: `npx agntc update` updates every installed plugin that can be updated; `npx agntc update owner/repo` updates that plugin, or every plugin of that collection; `npx agntc update owner/repo/plugin-name` updates one collection plugin. There is no interactive picker.
why: Follows the npm/brew convention.
rules_out: An interactive update picker

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: With no plugins installed, `update` displays "No plugins installed." and exits.
why: Nothing to update.

text: For a plugin installed from default HEAD (`ref: null`) or a branch (`ref: "dev"`), `update` runs `git ls-remote` for the HEAD or branch tip SHA and compares it with the stored `commit`: a difference means an update is available.
why: Smart comparison avoids unnecessary cloning.

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: A tag-pinned plugin is always up to date, as its tag resolves to the same commit forever; `update` checks for newer tags with `git ls-remote --tags` and informs the user, but never auto-upgrades it: the user re-adds with the new tag.
why: A pin is the user's explicit choice of version.
rules_out: Auto-upgrading tag-pinned plugins

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: A plugin installed from a local path gets no remote check: `update` always re-copies it from the stored path, with no change detection.
why: The tool can't tell whether local files changed, and an unconditional copy makes `update` a quick "refresh from source" during local plugin development.

text: `update` is nuke-and-reinstall: delete every file in the plugin's manifest `files`, re-clone at the same ref (HEAD for a null ref) or re-copy from the local path, re-copy for the same agents the manifest entry records, and update the manifest with the new commit SHA.
why: Handles renames, deletions and moves between versions without special logic.

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: `update` never re-prompts for agent selection; changing agents is a re-add.
why: Update means "latest version of what I already have".

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: `update` asks no confirmation.
why: Unlike `remove`, it is non-destructive in intent: the user asks for newer versions of what they already want, and the nuke is an implementation detail.

cites.section: What are the `update` semantics — per-plugin, per-repo, all-at-once? > Decision

text: `update` re-reads the new version's `agntc.json` and compares its `agents` with the manifest entry's. Where the author dropped some installed agents, it warns ("Plugin `{key}` no longer declares support for `{dropped_agent}`. Currently installed for: … New version supports: …"), installs only for agents still declared, lets the nuke remove the dropped agent's files without recreating them, updates the entry's `agents` to what was installed, and says so in the summary ("Updated for Claude. Codex support removed by plugin author — Codex files removed.").
why: Follows the author's declaration while telling the user what changed.

text: Where the new version supports none of the installed agents, `update` warns and skips that plugin ("Plugin `{key}` no longer supports any of your installed agents. No update performed. Run `npx agntc remove {key}` to clean up."), leaving the existing files in place.
why: The update would amount to a removal; the user decides when to remove.

text: `update` reports per plugin: updated plugins with old ref/SHA → new and asset counts per agent; up-to-date plugins with a brief acknowledgment; tag-pinned plugins with newer versions listing the available tags and the re-add command.
why: Each plugin's outcome is visible at a glance.

text: Should update checks be automated: check-on-next-command (any `npx agntc` invocation does a quick background SHA check and shows a banner, Homebrew-style) and/or an async Claude SessionStart hook writing a flag file (e.g. `.agntc/.updates-available`) for the next command to surface?

Research found manual `npx agntc update` already an improvement over the old `npm update` approach: scoped to plugins only, with no risk of updating unrelated project dependencies, and able to update all at once or one plugin (`npx agntc update owner/repo`).

cites.section: Manual update is already an improvement

text: Claude Marketplace checks for updates at session startup when auto-update is enabled, by git SHA comparison, and tells the user to restart; it has a known caching bug where the cache never refreshes (issue #17361).
how: Research into how Claude Marketplace handles updates.

text: Vercel Skills has no auto-update: updates are manual only (`npx skills check` / `npx skills update`), by GitHub tree SHA comparison.
how: Research into how Vercel Skills handles updates.

text: Research rejected, for now, a synchronous check in Claude Code's `SessionStart` hook: it can't add latency to startup, and context shouldn't be injected into Claude's session.
how: Research into Claude Code hooks.

text: Research identified two complementary approaches to automated update checks: check-on-next-command (universal; any `npx agntc` invocation does a quick background SHA check and shows a banner, like Homebrew, with zero overhead when the tool isn't used) and an async `SessionStart` hook (`"async": true`) that writes a flag file (e.g. `.agntc/.updates-available`) for the next `npx agntc` command to display. It left their tradeoffs and implementation details to discussion.
how: Research into Claude Code hooks and other tools' update checks.

text: The agent-hook approach to update checks is Claude-only for now: the other agents (Cursor, Cline, Codex) have no equivalent lifecycle hooks.

text: What should `list` show, and how?

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Context

text: `list` is an interactive management dashboard: view, update and remove all inline in one session, entered with `npx agntc list` and no arguments.
why: The manifest already holds everything a richer view needs, and @clack/prompts' `select()` and `spinner()` make it achievable without custom TUI work.
rules_out: A read-only dump of manifest state

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Decision

text: With no plugins installed, `list` displays "No plugins installed. Run `npx agntc add owner/repo` to get started." and exits.
why: Points the user at the first step.

text: `list` opens with a single "Checking for updates..." spinner over parallel `git ls-remote` checks for all installed plugins; local installs get no remote check.
why: Responsive for typical install sizes (2-10 plugins).

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Decision

text: Do the parallel `git ls-remote` checks stay responsive beyond typical install sizes, or will they need caching? Their responsiveness is asserted for 2-10 plugins, not measured, and caching is left for if latency becomes a problem at scale.

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Decision

text: `list` shows every installed plugin as a selectable list with "Done" at the bottom, whatever the count. Each row shows the plugin key, its ref where pinned to a tag or branch (nothing for HEAD), and a status indicator.
why: One view of everything installed and its state.

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Decision

text: `list`'s status indicators: `✓ Up to date` (default colour) for no update; `↑ Update available` (green) for a branch or HEAD with a newer commit; `⚑ Newer tags available` (yellow) for a tag pin with newer tags on the remote; `✗ Check failed` (red) when the remote couldn't be reached; `● Local` (default colour) for a local install.
why: Each update state reads at a glance.

text: Selecting a plugin opens a detail view: plugin key, ref (tag, branch or HEAD), commit SHA, install date, agents installed for, asset counts per agent, and the full file list.
why: Drill into one plugin from the list.

cites.section: What should `list` show and how? > Decision

text: The detail view's actions follow the update status: update available → Update, Remove, Back; up to date → Remove, Back; newer tags available → Change version, Remove, Back; check failed → Remove, Back; local → Update, Remove, Back.
why: Only actions that make sense for the plugin's state are offered.

text: Change version lists the available tags; picking one nuke-and-reinstalls at that tag and updates the manifest with the new ref and commit, the same mechanics as update with a new ref.
why: Gives tag-pinned plugins an upgrade path inside the dashboard.

text: `list`'s actions run inline, with the same mechanics as the standalone commands; Remove from `list` still shows its confirmation.
why: Consistency: remove always confirms, whatever the entry point.

why: The session continues with up-to-date state rather than exiting.

text: What does error handling look like: partial failures, network errors, git errors?

cites.section: What does error handling look like — partial failures, network errors, git errors? > Context

text: `remove` or `update` given a key matching no manifest entry displays "Plugin {key} is not installed." and exits non-zero, with no suggestions and no retry.
why: Fail fast on a bad argument.

text: `add` given a source that can't be resolved (invalid shorthand, unreachable URL) displays the git error clearly and exits non-zero.
why: Fail fast on a bad argument.

text: `add` given a local path that doesn't exist or isn't a directory displays "Path {path} does not exist or is not a directory." and exits non-zero.
why: Fail fast on a bad argument.

text: A clone failing on a transient error (network timeout, temporary git error) is retried up to 3 times; once retries are exhausted the git error is surfaced clearly and the operation aborts, with nothing to clean up as nothing was copied yet.
why: Retry transient failures, fail cleanly on hard ones.

cites.section: What does error handling look like — partial failures, network errors, git errors? > Decision

text: Auth failures (private repo, bad credentials) are not retried: the error surfaces immediately. The tool doesn't handle auth; it defers to the user's git configuration.
why: `git clone` already uses the user's SSH keys, credential helpers and tokens; if they have access it works.

cites.section: What does error handling look like — partial failures, network errors, git errors? > Decision

text: A local path that doesn't exist, isn't readable or holds no `agntc.json` surfaces a clear error and aborts.
why: Same principle as git errors: fail fast with a clear message.

text: A copy failing partway through a plugin rolls back to a clean state: everything copied so far for that plugin is deleted, as the `files` list tracked in memory during the copy names it, and no manifest entry is written.
why: A half-installed plugin is worse than none; better to fail cleanly and let the user retry.

cites.section: What does error handling look like — partial failures, network errors, git errors? > Decision

text: In a multi-plugin collection install each plugin is independent: one that succeeds keeps its manifest entry while one that fails (after retries) is rolled back, and the summary shows each plugin's outcome: installed, failed (with the error), or skipped (the user's choice on conflicts).
why: One plugin's failure shouldn't undo another's success.

cites.section: What does error handling look like — partial failures, network errors, git errors? > Decision

text: The spec is at odds with itself on whether a copy can overwrite another plugin's file: its rollback edge case accepts that a failed copy, after overwriting a file owned by another plugin, leaves that plugin's asset gone (restored by updating that plugin), while its cross-plugin collision rule makes any overlap with another plugin's file a hard block before copying, with no "install anyway" option, and its conflict handling says all conflict resolution happens before copying, so no rollback is needed. The edge case is left over from the log's dropped design of overwriting and transferring ownership in the manifest. No later source settles whether the edge case still applies.

text: File path collisions across plugins: is it a real risk when two plugins install assets to the same path, and how should agntc handle it?

Because the manifest tracks files per plugin, a plugin B overwriting plugin A's file means removing B deletes a file A thinks it owns, and with nuke-and-reinstall, updating either plugin overwrites the other's version.
how: Reasoned from the manifest's per-plugin file tracking and the nuke-and-reinstall update, as research flagged it.

cites.section: File path collisions across plugins — is this a real risk? > Context

text: Plugins are atomic and their assets interdependent (a skill may invoke a specific agent by name), so overwriting one asset of a plugin with another plugin's same-named file breaks that plugin's internal wiring: guaranteed breakage, not speculative damage. Renaming the incoming file (e.g. `review-2.md`) breaks the new plugin's references instead, since skills reference agents by filename; no resolution avoids breaking one side.
how: Reasoned in the discussion's journey from how plugin assets reference each other.

text: A file path collision with a file another plugin owns is a hard block on `add`: there is no "install anyway" option.
why: Plugins are atomic with interdependent assets; overwriting one asset from a plugin breaks the whole plugin's internal wiring, an objectively destructive outcome with no upside.
rules_out: Warning the user and letting them proceed ("advise, don't block")
Installing the colliding asset under another name (e.g. `review-2.md`)

cites.section: File path collisions across plugins — is this a real risk? > Decision

text: During `add`, before any copying or other file operation, the incoming file list is diffed against every existing manifest entry (a set intersection of paths); this check is separate from asset-level conflict handling.
why: The manifest already tracks exact file paths per plugin, so detection is cheap.

cites.section: File path collisions across plugins — is this a real risk? > Decision

text: On a collision, agntc shows which files conflict and which plugin owns them, and offers exactly two options: remove the conflicting plugin first and then continue the install, handled in one flow with no separate commands, or cancel.
why: Overwriting is destructive with no upside, so no third option is offered.

text: Asset rename or delete between versions: when a plugin author renames or deletes an asset, how does nuke-and-reinstall handle it, given the user's agent config or custom files may reference the old name?

cites.section: Asset rename/delete between versions — how does nuke-and-reinstall handle this? > Context

text: Nuke-and-reinstall handles asset renames and deletions with no additional tooling: update deletes every path in the entry's manifest `files`, re-clones (or re-copies from the local path) and copies fresh assets, then rewrites the entry with the new file list, so a renamed asset's old file is deleted and its new one created, a deleted asset is never re-created, and the manifest reflects what is on disk after the update.
why: Deleting everything recorded and copying what the new version ships covers renames, deletions and moved files without special logic.

text: What shape does a refusal take, and what happens to a part of a line agntc cannot honour?

A refusal is always pre-flight: the command exits non-zero, writes nothing (no installed files, no manifest entry) and removes nothing, and its message names what was refused and the way through where one exists.
why: A refusal that exited 0 would read as success to an AI agent caller, which acts on the exit status rather than the text; it takes the shape of configless-install's pre-flight failures.

text: Never silently ignore: no part of a line (a flag, a source form, a name) is silently dropped. Where Vercel ignores or drops something without saying so, agntc refuses instead — unknown flags, and names that match nothing or only partly match.
why: The scope's rule that a pasted line is never met by a silently ignored part.

text: What makes an agntc install equivalent to Vercel's — the same behaviour, or the same files in the same places?

An install is equivalent when the skill behaves the same for the agent; the files need not sit where Vercel puts them. agntc keeps a real copy per agent in each agent's own directory — Claude `.claude/skills/`, Codex `.agents/skills/`, Cursor `.cursor/skills/` — and does not adopt Vercel's canonical `.agents/skills` copy with symlinks from each agent's directory.
why: A skill behaves the same from a copy or a link, and matching the layout would have agntc tracking shared files and links; the layout matters only where Vercel's own tools touch an agntc install. Per-agent copies also hold cursor-agent-driver's rule that each agent owns its directory.
alternatives: Match Vercel's canonical store with symlink fan-out
